X4: Foundations — Effective-Play Guide Summary

This summary is derived strictly from a community player's account of roughly 200 hours of play (about 50 of them without mods), and reflects that player's own experience and opinions rather than confirmed developer statements. Where the source expresses uncertainty, opinion, or a recent balance change, that framing is preserved below.

On Modding

The source strongly recommends playing with mods, arguing that the unmodified AI is weak enough, and asset organization limited enough, that mods meaningfully reduce frustration. A distinction is drawn between mods considered mild UI/quality-of-life improvements the author feels should arguably be part of the base game, and a second group of "progression-altering" mods that shift pacing somewhat but are judged worth the tradeoff. Mods are available via Steam Workshop or Nexus Mods.

Quality-of-life mods mentioned: UI Extensions and HUD; UI Trade Analytics (which enables station profiles such as a "Factory" profile); Custom Tabs (for organizing assets into custom UI tabs); Equipment Tooltips; Better Target Monitor; KUDA AI tweaks; Surface Element Targeting; TaterTrade; Sector Patrol (which can also be used, per the source, to have a ship "attack stations" as a way of locating hidden installations); and Sector Explorer (for automating scout-ship exploration).

Progression-altering mods mentioned: Satellite Service, which reduces the tedium of placing satellites and resource probes but is described as somewhat immersion-breaking; Fly-by Looting, which eases loot collection, possibly to excess; Builders Can Haul (elsewhere called "Builders Can Carry" in the same source), which gives builder ships much larger cargo storage and enables docking medium ships on a builder to form a "Special Transport Fleet"; 10x Modules, under which one station module functions as ten with a build time of about 1 minute — called the single biggest improvement on the list, since an unmodded large late-game station can otherwise take up to roughly a full real-world day to build; Friendly Fire Tweaks, which can be abused somewhat but addresses friendly-fire aggro the source considers excessive in the base game; Inventory Collector, which automates gathering inventory from the player's other ships; and Faster Crew Leveling, which speeds up what the source calls an "absurdly slow" base-game crew leveling rate.

Early Game

Early moneymaking options are, in the source's assessment, limited. Pirating ships is presented as the strongest method for building early credits and fleet size. A second option, informally called being a "trash panda," involves looting active faction-conflict zones while avoiding stray missiles; this can be improved by keeping a transport ship nearby to gather larger drops, and the source notes stations under attack by an opposing faction often drop valuable items (sometimes requiring a black market trader to sell). This looting strategy is reported to have been recently nerfed. A related tactic is destroying transport ships carrying valuable cargo (Claytronics is given as an example) through neutral territory, which requires having a player-owned transport ship ready to collect the resulting drop. Asteroid crystal mining is described as having been heavily nerfed, now yielding roughly 100,000 credits about once per hour.

Scanning stations is recommended early on, both for uncovering early missions and for progress toward unlocking the Personal Headquarters (PHQ), which the source treats as a top early priority. Main missions for factions such as Hatikvah (HAT), and the DLC factions Terrans (TER) and Split (SPL), are described as offering good rewards, though completing them may require credits. General sector exploration is framed as enjoyable and useful for revealing the map and factions, but not profitable; pairing a scout ship with the Sector Explorer mod's automated behavior is suggested to save time. The source separately expresses frustration that pirating is essentially the only lucrative combat-based path for most of the game.

Later Early Game

Once a player has roughly 500,000–1,000,000 credits, the source recommends shifting toward passive income via medium miners or transport ships. Miners should be placed near a refinery for ore and/or silicon, or near a graphene source for gas mining, with mineral mining suggested as likely more profitable than gas. Recommended miner loadout: combat engines, as full a crew as possible, and (for mineral mining) the best affordable mining laser; ships should be chosen for good cargo capacity and speed.

Transport ships should be set up to buy low and sell high, a workflow the source says the DeadTater tool/mod automates; medium transports should be based in a refinery-adjacent sector not far from the highway loop. Trade ships and mining ships are both described as effective, low-risk ways to level crew and pilots. Drop ships and inventory collectors, ideally using scout ships, are framed as more valuable for crafting-material access than for direct credits, and are best used after the PHQ is obtained, to avoid illegal wares accumulating in inventory.

Mid Game

Around 5,000,000 credits, the source recommends building energy stations and refineries in areas with strong sunlight and good ore/gas yields, citing The Reach as an example sector. Stations should be placed as close to a jump gate as possible; plots can be rotated by right-click to improve alignment. A minimal effective starting build is a dock, container storage, and energy cell production.

Satellites and resource probes are recommended almost universally at this stage. The source states that miners without a resource probe within roughly 40 km suffer a 50 percent mining penalty. Silicon is described as usually the most profitable and sustainable resource to mine, while also being the hardest to mine. Scanning stations for blueprints, once unlocked via research, is presented as a good use of time and a way to save credits.

Energy stations are also framed as a way to improve faction relationships, since DeadTater-run couriers trading energy cells raise reputation passively. Docking rights with a faction must be unlocked before trading with it. To raise reputation from -15 (or lower) to -9, the source describes killing "enemy" ships that spawn outside a faction's stations, then moving to the next station once a per-station cooldown is hit. From -9 up to roughly +10/+15, the source describes buying 100–200 units of medicine or food and selling them one at a time to the faction's wharf or shipyard — a tactic it calls "cheesing," which works because the reputation gain per trade is fixed regardless of price or volume; the ship performing these trades cannot undock until they finish.

Whether to convert an energy station into a refinery, or simply build another energy station, is framed as depending on whether local refineries are actually buying the raw material being mined. Player-owned refineries should have a trade rule (set under Global Orders → Player Information) restricting raw-material purchases to the player's own faction. Refined goods should initially be priced below market rate so AI ships come to buy them, avoiding the overhead of running a dedicated trade fleet; the in-game trade overlay (with filters) can be used to check current prices.

Later Mid Game

Relying on AI-driven purchases to move goods elsewhere is said to sacrifice roughly 20 percent or more of potential price compared to self-directed export. At this stage the source recommends using the Custom Tabs mod with at least three tabs — Production, Supply, and Distribution — with refineries placed in Production.

DeadTater is described as supporting four primary transport roles: supplying a station manager's build storage, acting as a sector supply captain, acting as a sector distribution captain, and repeat-ordering specific wares. At this stage the source focuses mainly on the build-storage and sector-distribution-captain roles. A typical sector distribution captain is set with its home sector at the refinery, a buy range of 0 jumps, a sell range of 4 jumps, "Prefer my sell orders" enabled, and a minimum capacity threshold of 80 percent; supplying a sector is described as the inverse setup.

Combined with UI Trade Analytics station profiles, refineries are recommended to use the "Factory" profile. The source suggests initially leaving the sell restriction off refined goods (letting other factions buy directly), since the player's own transport fleet likely can't move full volume yet, and later reinstating the restriction or building a dedicated factory outlet station as the player's own trade network matures. It's also recommended to hold back credits for sector defense frigates and corvettes as new threats emerge.

Late Mid Game

The stated goal at this point is full self-sufficiency, driven by dissatisfaction with faction ship prices. In a Commonwealth-economy playthrough, this means building a hull parts and claytronics factory near or attached to the refineries. For a full shipyard build (assuming the 10x Modules mod) targeting under 300,000,000 credits, the source estimates needing roughly 30 claytronics modules and 50 hull parts modules. Self-supplying claytronics is described as the single highest-value move available at this stage.

Building independent factories for other, non-claytronics/hull-parts wares is considered not especially valuable by the source, since simply selling refined materials is said to capture about 80 percent of the benefit for about 20 percent of the effort — each additional factory adds transport overhead. Shipyard placement should favor an area rich in ore and silicon with reasonable proximity to methane, described as the biggest constraints on output; the recommended build order is refineries, then intermediates, then advanced resources. A shipyard blueprint then allows building ships from parts sourced anywhere, at no extra cost once owned.

The source states that, in the base game, selling player-built ships to factions is capped at a maximum of 70 percent of listed price even though the sell-price slider can be set up to 150 percent — calling the slider misleading — and recommends leaving the slider at 150 percent regardless, since factions will still buy at the effective cap. Mods reportedly exist to remove this cap. Selling ships to a given faction requires owning that faction's part blueprints, since factions won't buy ships mixing components from multiple factions; owning all small and medium ship blueprints is said to increase order volume. Shipyard sales can be restricted via blacklist to allied factions only, or opened to everyone (which may cause factions to fight near the shipyard).

The source separately describes — while expressing some discomfort with the fact that it works — a "proxy war" exploit: building a shipyard near an enemy defense station, blacklisting sales to enemies only, supplying it with distribution and trade ships, and keeping a player-owned defense station in the sector to seize the target once the AI destroys it, all without incurring a reputation penalty.

Late Game

Late game is described as an open sandbox / conquest phase. The source's Custom Tabs setup expands to: Core (special-operations and manually controlled build/military fleets), Production (factories, refineries), Supply (supply stations and fleets), Distribution (distribution stations and fleets), Defense (defense stations, sector patrol fleets, quick-response fleets), Scouting (exploration and satellite-service ships), Teleport (ships stationed near faction representatives), and Spaced (floating space suits recovered from battles).

A ship-naming strategy using loadout names is recommended, potentially one loadout name per station a group of ships commonly serves. An example given is "XVG SY1 Mineral [DP]" applied to a Crane, decoded as: XVG = player faction tag, SY1 = shipyard 1, Mineral = mining role, and [DP] = a "don't pickup" tag used to avoid issues with a capital-ship loot-magnet mod. Shipyards are named in the format [Faction Tag] [Identifier][Number], e.g. "XVG SY1."

End Notes and Miscellaneous Tips

The source notes that a full playthrough can easily run into the hundreds of hours, much of it spent in menus, and recommends managing the empire while riding a moving ship or from an observation deck; F2 plus the numpad arrow keys and +/- provide camera pan/zoom for this. The source separately wishes fleet-combat rendering distance were configurable, calling large-scale battles visually disappointing as currently rendered.

Additional tips recorded: keep a dedicated "pilot transfer" ship docked, periodically moving five-star pilots off medium trade/mining ships onto it (promoting a replacement pilot each time), to build a pool of future ship captains; assigning liked pilots to the marines category avoids unwanted voice lines during boarding or when handing off a personal ship to a captain; defense platforms can be built near jump gates by placing a small plot close to the gate and then expanding it to encompass the gate, taking care not to block it; the game supports pause, quicksave, and quickload; AI enemies will never attempt to board the player's ships, so marines are unnecessary except on ships meant for boarding; fully crewed ships perform better; pilot skill matters more than crew skill, with a five-star pilot and base-tier crew yielding a ship rated at a minimum of 3.5 stars.

On the Global Orders page (trade rules, blacklists, alerts), the source recommends: a trade rule restricting trades to the player's own faction; a default civilian travel blacklist covering dangerous regions and enemy-owned sectors; and alerts for large/extra-large Xenon ships (ideally scoped to sectors bordering Xenon space) and for Kha'ak. Repeated Kha'ak attacks on a sector are attributed to a Kha'ak installation station present in that sector, which will keep generating attacks until destroyed (requiring at least one destroyer); it can be located by exploring the sector's edges with a fast ship, using long-range scans, or via the Sector Patrol mod's "attack stations" behavior. The source further states that Kha'ak hives exist in certain sectors every game, and destroying a hive stops or greatly reduces installations spawning in neighboring sectors, pointing to an external forum thread (https://forum.egosoft.com/viewtopic.php?t=443020) for more detail.

Using the Builders Can Carry mod, a "Special Transport Fleet" can be formed by docking several medium ships (the source's example: ten Vulture Sentinels) on one builder, undocking them to fill cargo (including the builder's own hold), redocking, traveling to the destination, and unloading — a technique the source uses for building shipyards with Terran materials far from Terran space and for bootstrapping defense stations, typically escorted by frigates that the source says are rarely actually needed in practice.

Finally, the source notes that player factories require sufficient credits in the station account for the trade logic to execute purchases, even for trades within the player's own faction, since the game checks affordability regardless of actual cost; an underfunded account can result in symptoms like a freighter delivering only a handful of units (e.g. 5 energy cells) because that's all the account could nominally afford. Suggested safe minimums are roughly 1,000,000 credits for small operations and 10,000,000 for larger ones; the same funding requirement applies to build storage, though the source notes a deliberately low build-storage balance can serve as a useful bottleneck given limited docking space, whereas overfunding it can create long queues of waiting trader ships.

Source's Recommended Ships, Weapons, Engines, and Shields

Ships (by role): Fighter — Moreya (DLC); Heavy Fighter — Shin (DLC); Corvette — Kuraokami (DLC); Frigate — Cobra (DLC); Gunboat — Jian (DLC); Transport — Boa (DLC), and either Shuyaki or Pelican depending on distance; Miner — Manorina (DLC) and Crane; Carrier — Shark (DLC); Builder — Heracles (contingent on using the Builders Can Carry mod). The source states there is no single best destroyer given the tradeoffs involved, but names Syn and Odysseus as both working well.

Weapons: pulse lasers and shard batteries for interceptor roles against fighters and small/light-medium ships; plasma, ion, and (with resupply tolerance) torpedoes for larger medium ships through destroyers; ARG flak for medium turrets (chosen for tracking speed); PAR plasma for large turrets against capital ships, and beam weapons for large turrets against fighters (noted as largely ineffective against bigger targets).

Engines: as a rule of thumb, combat engines for anything below L class except scouts, since combat engines help miners and transports evade pirates and navigate asteroid fields (where travel drives frequently cancel). Both Split and Terran combat engines are rated highly — Terran for very fast travel-drive acceleration, Split for very fast base speed. The source personally uses Terran engines roughly 80 percent of the time, for economic reasons tied to running a mixed Commonwealth/Terran shipyard. For travel drives, Argon or Terran are recommended; for most L and XL ships, the All Round engine is considered best.

Shields: Terran (TER) shields are called almost objectively the best option. Argon (ARG) and Terran are both described as "middle ground" shields, but Terran is said to outperform Argon on every metric. Paranid (PAR) shields offer slightly faster recharge than Terran at the cost of capacity, while Teladi (TEL) shields offer slightly more capacity than Terran at the cost of recharge time.
